A.explanation: Linear decrease on PQ, horizontal constant speed on QR, then steeper linear increase on RS with final speed similar to initial speed.

B.explanation: Speed continues to fall slowly along horizontal QR, but with no friction and no slope there is no acceleration so $v$ must stay constant.

C.explanation: Final speed after descending to S is much larger than starting speed at P, but P and S are at similar heights so energy conservation requires similar speeds.

D.explanation: Speed starts at zero and increases throughout, whereas the ball starts with maximum speed at P and slows while climbing PQ.

hints: Notice the three sections in order: gentle up-slope PQ, flat top QR, then steeper down-slope RS.
Recall that gradient of a $v$-$t$ graph is acceleration, which on a frictionless slope is set by the component of weight along the slope.
Compare the expected $v$ shape: steady fall then flat then steady rise, with a steeper rise on RS and a final $v$ close to the starting $v$.
walkthrough: Split the motion from P to S into PQ, QR and RS. The surface is frictionless so only the component of weight along the motion changes the speed.
On up-slope PQ the component acts down the slope, giving constant negative acceleration. So $v$ falls linearly with time with a shallow gradient because PQ is gentle.
On horizontal QR there is no component along the motion, so acceleration is zero. So $v$ is constant and the $v$-$t$ graph is horizontal.
On down-slope RS the component acts down the slope, giving constant positive acceleration. So $v$ rises linearly, and the gradient is steeper than on PQ because RS is steeper.

Since P and S finish at about the same height and there is no friction loss, kinetic energy and hence speed at S must be close to that at P. Only the graph with fall, flat middle, and steeper rise back to near the start fits. This is option A.
